channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Bill Gates foresees massive AI job loss: these VCs disagree | E2330
gist: On This Week in VC, Jason Calacanis hosts Shiel Mohnot, Dave McClure, and Hussein Kanji to debate Bill Gates' AI-jobs essay, dissect Meta's $17.1B kids' safety settlement, chart the explosive growth of private-market tenders vs. IPOs, unpack the Stripe/OpenRouter and Cursor deals, and share live portfolio marks in robotics, AI accounting, and drug discovery.

themes.theme: AI and the Jobs Displacement Debate

insights.claim: Bill Gates published a 6,000-word essay, 'The Turbulent AI Era Is Here,' arguing AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented or the worst source of injustice, that AI risks are currently outpacing its benefits across law, medicine and software, and that there is 'no plan' yet to manage the transition.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis (summarizing Bill Gates)
insights.so_what: A prominent tech elder statesman publicly calling for AI usage taxes and reserved human-only jobs signals rising odds of AI-specific regulation and redistribution policy.
insights.quote: AI will quote either be the greatest equalizer ever invented or the worst source of injustice and that right now quote there is no plan.

insights.claim: Dave McClure says he broadly agrees with three of Gates' core points: some jobs will permanently disappear, bad actors get 'superpowers' from AI (already visible with cheap drones), and there are real risks to kids and human connection.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A working VC partially endorsing the doom case suggests the debate isn't just hype-skeptics vs. Gates; there is real overlap in the investor community.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji argues job displacement is fundamentally a human coordination problem, not an AI problem, and is skeptical the world can coordinate a response given its track record on nuclear proliferation and climate change.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: If coordinated global policy is unlikely, investors should assume displacement plays out unmanaged and look for market-based (not regulatory) solutions and hedges.
insights.quote: This is not a new topic... this is a human problem not an AI problem and maybe you know the keys over to the AI maybe they might do a better job.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji predicts that if the 'a dollar of compute equals $10 of intelligence' ratio holds, it is only a matter of time before higher-cognition white-collar work, not just routine tasks, gets automated away.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Frames a testable economic ratio investors can track (compute cost vs. labor substitution value) as a leading indicator for which white-collar categories get automated next.
insights.quote: if you really believe this idea that like a dollar of compute equals, you know, $10 of intelligence, it's I think it's only a matter of time before even the higher cognition things in society kind of get replaced.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot says the data currently shows fast job displacement in knowledge industries but no visible displacement yet in physical/blue-collar work; he estimates gig-delivery jobs (e.g. DoorDash driving) are safe for roughly the next 5 years, disagreeing with Dave McClure's 10-year estimate.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: Gives investors a rough timeline (5 vs 10 years) for when physical/gig-labor automation actually shows up in employment data, useful for sizing robotics/delivery-automation bets.
insights.quote: I think you know we're seeing job displacement in knowledge industries very fast but like physical You're not seeing it in the data.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis observes that companies like Microsoft, Google, Uber, and Facebook have kept roughly flat headcount over the last 5 years (+/- 10%) while earnings grew 30-40% and revenue grew 10-20%, which he attributes to AI making existing employees far more productive rather than net job cuts so far.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable pattern (flat headcount + rising earnings) that public-market investors can use as an early AI-productivity signal in mega-cap tech financials.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues Jensen Huang's framing is correct for white-collar work -- 'you're not going to have your job replaced by AI, you're going to have your job replaced by somebody using AI' -- but believes blue-collar and gig work (delivery, driving) face straightforward job loss with no equivalent AI-augmentation path.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Splits the jobs debate into two distinct investable theses: AI-augmentation tools for knowledge workers vs. automation that fully displaces physical/gig labor.
insights.quote: You're not going to have your job replaced by AI. You're going to have your job replaced by somebody using AI.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot and Dave McClure predict a boom in solo proprietorships and one-person businesses because AI now automates the admin work (scheduling, billing, follow-ups) that used to require hiring extra staff -- e.g., a therapist no longer needs a receptionist.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot / Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Points to a large addressable market for AI back-office tools sold to solo operators and micro-businesses rather than only enterprise.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts a 'Cambrian explosion' in solo entrepreneurship among the current college generation, because students already fluent in using AI to 'cheat' through school are well positioned to run AI agents to build companies, just as corporate entry-level hiring dries up.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Suggests seed investors should expect a wave of very young, AI-native solo founders as an alternative to a shrinking corporate entry-level job market.
insights.quote: I think we'll see a Cambrian explosion in sole proprietorships because you're just not going to have four job offers.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts that within the next two years, US progressive politicians will respond to gig-worker anger over AI/robotaxi displacement by pushing capped, auctioned licenses for self-driving and delivery vehicles (e.g., starting around $30,000), modeling China's approach of capping robotaxi permits in Wuhan, Beijing and Shanghai after unrest among underemployed young drivers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete regulatory tail risk for autonomous-vehicle and delivery-robotics business models: license caps and auction fees that raise the cost of deploying fleets in progressive US cities.
insights.quote: I bet you we see AOC and Mandami and Boston and DC, LA just say, you know what, if you want a self-driving car license... you just need a license. The licenses are auctioned off at $30,000 starting price.

themes.theme: Policy and Redistribution Responses to AI

insights.claim: Dave McClure argues a federal 'token tax' is a bad long-term policy because token costs are trending toward zero, meaning it would tax a rapidly diminishing revenue base; he says the real fix is capex depreciation rules that currently make it cheaper for firms to buy AI/agent infrastructure than to hire humans.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Warns policymakers and investors that per-token taxation schemes are structurally self-defeating as inference costs fall; tax policy on capex/depreciation is the more durable lever.
insights.quote: I think that's a great idea because token costs are going down to zero. So, you're going to be taxing a diminishing return asset.

insights.claim: Dave McClure frames the needed policy response as a 'New Deal for the AI era,' but oriented around human-centric services -- a care economy for seniors, arts and culture -- rather than physical infrastructure, plus retraining and support budgets for displaced workers.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Identifies care-economy and human-services sectors as places AI may create policy-subsidized demand even as it displaces jobs elsewhere -- a potential investment theme.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot argues broad token taxes are wrong because they discourage beneficial AI adoption; instead governments should tax excess monopoly profits of AI labs and real externalities like power usage (he supports a per-mile robotaxi tax) but dismisses AI water-usage concerns as overstated next to agricultural water use.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: Lays out a more investor-friendly tax framework (target profits/externalities, not usage) that would be less damaging to AI-native business models than blanket token levies.
insights.quote: if these companies have enormous excess profits that concentrates wealth, then tax the excess profits.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot floats the idea that government could take roughly a 10% equity stake in Anthropic and OpenAI to help pay down the national debt, comparing it to the pattern of the Trump administration extracting equity stakes from companies via pressure.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: A live idea circulating among VCs that could presage government equity demands on frontier AI labs as a condition of scale or favorable treatment.
insights.quote: let's take 10% of anthropic and open AI and solve our national debt problem.

insights.claim: Dave McClure counters that state equity stakes in frontier AI labs create a governance conflict, since government would then have a financial incentive to go easy on regulating companies it partly owns.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A structural argument against sovereign-equity-in-AI-labs proposals that investors evaluating regulatory risk should weigh.

insights.claim: Dave McClure argues Norway's success managing its oil wealth (versus Venezuela's failure) traces back to pre-existing institutions -- it had already built a competitive hydropower and timber/shipbuilding industry before oil was discovered -- implying rule-of-law and prior institutional capacity, not the resource windfall itself, determine whether an 'AI dividend' would be well managed.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Cautions against assuming a national AI wealth fund would automatically benefit citizens broadly; outcome depends heavily on existing governance quality.

themes.theme: Meta's $17.1B Settlement and the Social Media/Kids Debate

insights.claim: Meta agreed to a $17.1 billion settlement with 29 state attorneys general over claims it hooked kids on Instagram and Facebook, including scroll-interrupt prompts at 15/60/90 minutes, a midnight-to-6am usage block, no push notifications from 8am-3pm during school hours, mandatory age verification, redesign of harm-linked features like beauty filters and visible like-counts, anti-bullying safeguards, and independent audits.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Sets a detailed regulatory template and cost/feature baseline that other social platforms may now be pressured to adopt.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji argues the $17.1B fine, while the largest ever for a tech company, is small relative to Meta's market cap and free cash flow (he estimates roughly 10% of annual FCF), and Meta's stock actually rose more than 1% on the news -- meaning the settlement effectively 'paid for itself.'
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Suggests headline-grabbing regulatory fines may not meaningfully change platform incentives if markets treat them as immaterial to valuation.
insights.quote: Meta stock is up... probably larger than 17 billion is if I'm going to guess it went up more than 1% on settlement so it paid for itself.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot (disclosing his wife works at Instagram as a lawyer) states Instagram self-implemented a teen sleep mode (10pm-7am) and automatic 60-minute usage notifications roughly two years before this settlement; the main change from the settlement is applying these policies uniformly across Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: Complicates the narrative that Meta only acted under legal pressure -- some protective features predate the settlement, relevant for assessing platform self-regulation credibility.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot argues the public discourse on social media harm is one-sided, crediting real mental-health benefits (citing his own experience using social media to combat isolation during COVID) and teen creative outlets that rarely get discussed, and compares the industry's PR problem to AI's.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: A reminder that headline regulatory/harm narratives can obscure offsetting benefits investors should weigh when valuing consumer social platforms.
insights.quote: Social media cured me, I think, like from depression.

insights.claim: Dave McClure recounts that Steve Jobs privately told him he did not let his own young kids use iPhones/iPads at the age Dave's kids were using them, despite Apple building and selling the devices.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A recurring pattern among tech insiders of privately restricting their own children's access to products they publicly promote -- relevant color for the kids-safety debate.
insights.quote: Later, I found out he didn't allow his own kids to have access to bones at that age.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis ranks social media alongside tobacco, alcohol, and processed/sugary foods as among the most addictive products ever created, adding screen-related mental health harms as a fourth major societal cost.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames social-media regulation as likely to follow the same decades-long trajectory as tobacco/alcohol regulation -- useful for modeling long-run regulatory risk on consumer attention platforms.
insights.quote: Tobacco, alcohol, and carbs.

themes.theme: Private Markets: The New Illiquid IPO Economy

insights.claim: Dave McClure's data shows $100M+ private funding rounds overtook $100M+ IPOs starting around 2016 (the SoftBank Vision Fund era); currently there are roughly 400 private $100M+ rounds per year versus only about 40-50 IPOs of that size, a roughly 10-to-1 ratio.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far private capital has outpaced public listings, reinforcing that companies now must be worth $500M-$1B+ before going public.

insights.claim: Dave McClure's data shows corporate tender offers (companies buying back employee/early-investor shares) grew from about $6.5B (2023) to $12B (2024) to an estimated $27-37B (2025), more than doubling year over year, and calls it 'the new IPO market' for liquidity at companies like Databricks and Stripe.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Identifies a fast-growing, underappreciated market (secondary tenders) as the real liquidity channel for late-stage employees, relevant for anyone pricing pre-IPO shares.
insights.quote: This is really the new IPO market. This is like where liquidity is coming from for employees.

insights.claim: Dave McClure notes the largest private companies (SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe tier) typically sell only about 2-5% of their cap table per tender round despite being worth hundreds of billions, letting founders retain overwhelming control while still offering employees some liquidity.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Shows how mega-cap private companies stay private almost indefinitely without diluting control, changing how long-duration equity value accrues to insiders vs. outside investors.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji argues retail investors are the biggest structural losers of the stay-private-longer trend: in the 1990s the public could buy shares at $100-300M market caps, but today they can't access equity until valuations are enormous, and there is no required quarterly financial disclosure on private secondary marketplaces (Forge, EquityZen, etc.), so buyers are 'flying blind.'
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Highlights an information-asymmetry risk for anyone buying private secondary shares in hot AI names without audited financials.
insights.quote: Everybody's flying blind and buying that on Vibes.

insights.claim: Dave McClure warns many seed and early-stage funds are sitting on high paper markups (3-5x TVPI) but near-zero DPI after 10-year fund lifespans, and floats a hypothetical roll-up strategy -- raising ~$500M to acquire struggling growth-stage startups, cut 80-90% of costs like Elon did at Twitter, and turn them profitable, similar to what Bending Spoons does.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Flags an emerging LP liquidity crisis in venture and a concrete counter-strategy (roll-up/PE-style acquisitions of underperforming VC-backed startups) that could become its own asset class.
insights.quote: you can do what Elon did at Twitter, you know, get rid of 80, 90% of the cost and now you've got a wonderful business.

insights.claim: The panel notes Headspace was reportedly sold to Sword Health for roughly $200-300M cash, down about 90% from its last private valuation mark of $3 billion, echoing the earlier Airtable markdown from a rumored $10B mark, as evidence of a broader 'SaaS apocalypse' among 2021-era unicorns.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure / Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that steady-growth-but-not-venture-scale companies from the 2021 boom are being marked down 80-90% in actual exits, a warning for anyone still holding 2021-vintage paper marks.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot pushes back on Chamath Palihapitiya's claim that Silicon Valley has lost its founding idealism and only cares about money now, arguing it is 'most likely a function of who Chamath surrounds himself with,' and pointing to people at Anthropic and OpenAI who are already wealthy but continue working as evidence mission-driven motivation persists.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: A direct rebuttal to a widely circulated 'Valley has lost its soul' narrative, arguing the mission-driven culture at leading AI labs is real, not performative.
insights.quote: most likely a function of who Jamal surrounds him with.

insights.claim: Dave McClure partially disagrees, noting that unlike the late-1990s dot-com era, today founders and early employees routinely take large secondary liquidity (millions of dollars) at the seed and Series A stage, making the industry structurally 'much more coin-operated' than it was 20-30 years ago.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Identifies early secondary liquidity as a structural driver of changed founder incentives, useful context for LPs evaluating why founders today may exit or de-risk earlier than prior generations.
insights.quote: it becomes much more coin operated than than it used to be in the past.

themes.theme: Big Deals: Stripe/OpenRouter, Cursor, and xAI

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji frames Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter as infrastructure-buying-infrastructure: Stripe, the plumbing layer for payments, is acquiring the plumbing/information layer for AI token spend, giving it visibility into how money flows through the AI economy -- a strategic logic he compares to the (retrospectively obvious) Google/YouTube and Meta/WhatsApp acquisitions.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Suggests payments infrastructure companies may increasingly acquire AI-inference routing/metering layers as a strategic land-grab on where AI spend actually flows.
insights.quote: it's the information layer. You kind of know exactly how the token spends kind of going through the economy.

insights.claim: Panel discusses Stripe paying roughly $7-8 billion for OpenRouter, a company reportedly doing only around $100-200M in revenue, implying a 50-100x revenue multiple, just months after OpenRouter had raised at a $1.3 billion valuation; Ramp launched a competing product (router.com) the same day the deal was announced.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot / panel
insights.so_what: Signals extreme valuation premiums on AI-infrastructure routing layers and shows how fast incumbents (Ramp) can spin up competing products, raising defensibility questions.
insights.quote: between 50 and 100 times is unbelievable.

insights.claim: Dave McClure notes Cursor (Anysphere) produced one of the largest venture outcomes ever: Andreessen Horowitz invested roughly $44-60M and got back about $6.6 billion, a ~150x return, while early investor Ali Partovi (Neo) reportedly put in about $1.5M and stands to get back billions.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Illustrates the scale of power-law outlier returns concentrating in a small number of AI-native developer-tool bets this cycle.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis notes Y Combinator publicly attacked Cursor's founder-investor origin story around the time of its huge outcome (Cursor never went through YC), and Dave McClure says YC did something similar to him after he left 500 Startups -- both frame it as YC treating outside-accelerator success as a competitive threat.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis / Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Suggests accelerator brand politics intensify around outsized non-YC outcomes, relevant color for founders weighing accelerator affiliation.
insights.quote: I can tell you from experience it's a very different thing when you are not competing with YC and are competing.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis characterizes xAI as having been largely a shell company valuable mainly for Elon Musk's infrastructure and capex (much of it rented out to Anthropic and Google) rather than its technology, but credits Musk's pivot over the last 6-9 months for creating a new 'Elon web services' compute-rental revenue line that could become the company's majority revenue source.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Reframes xAI's value proposition away from model quality toward compute-rental infrastructure, a different competitive lens than typical frontier-lab comparisons.
insights.quote: XAI was a shell of a company that was mostly valuable because of Elon infrastructure and cabex that Elon bought.

themes.theme: Physical AI and the Robotics Frontier

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji observes venture sentiment has flipped from anti-hardware to pro-hardware in about five years, because in a software world where frontier language models are increasingly consolidated among a few labs, hardware's inherent difficulty is now seen as a source of defensibility rather than a reason to avoid a sector.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Marks a structural shift in VC risk appetite: capital-intensive hardware moats are back in favor as a defense against commoditized software/models.
insights.quote: It's amazing how this industry has transformed from being anti-hardware 5 years ago to very very very pro hardware across the board.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji believes it remains genuinely open who wins 'transformers for physical [robotics]' and 'transformers for biology,' unlike language models where the frontier-lab field is largely settled; he discloses a stealth robotics investment out of Imperial College launching in about 2-3 months that uses a technique requiring far less training data than large generalist robotics models.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: Flags robotics and biology as the next open frontier-model land grabs, in contrast to language models where the competitive set is already fixed.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot describes Skild AI's (a Carnegie Mellon spinout) robotics demo showing a robot flipping pancakes perfectly every time and a robot dog relearning to walk after losing part of a leg, calling it evidence of fast-generalizing robot learning; he says early-stage physical-AI checks at his fund (~$2-2.5M average) burn through in about 9 months given robotics' capital intensity.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: Physical-AI startups consume capital much faster than typical software seed rounds, meaning check sizes and follow-on cadence must be underwritten differently.

insights.claim: The panel estimates humanoid robot bill-of-materials cost at roughly $15-20K, priced to consumers around $20-30K -- comparable to a Toyota Prius -- and argues that price point makes robots an easy purchase given the household labor they'd replace (Jason says he'd pay $100K+ for one that reliably cleans and cooks).
insights.speaker: panel (Jason Calacanis, Shiel Mohnot)
insights.so_what: A concrete unit-economics anchor (BOM ~$15-20K, retail ~$20-30K) for modeling consumer humanoid robotics adoption and margin potential.
insights.quote: I think they're the cost of a Toyota Prius.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says Elon Musk privately showed him a newer, faster-moving Optimus robot on his phone (not shown publicly), a visible improvement from what Jason saw six months earlier at the Optimus lab, and predicts Musk will 'make a billion' of them for tasks like agricultural harvesting, which could crash commodity prices (e.g., strawberries down to $0.25-1/lb).
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: First-hand signal that Optimus's capability is progressing faster privately than shown publicly, with a specific downstream prediction (commodity deflation in labor-intensive agriculture) investors could position around.
insights.quote: If a million of those were out there, you know, planting strawberries, like the price of strawberries is going to be a dollar a pound, 25 cents a pound.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot describes Instinct, an AI personal-assistant startup (seed backed by Conviction and reportedly Kleiner Perkins), which stores users' payment info in a 'vault' so it can autonomously complete tasks like actually booking a flight rather than just pointing to a booking page; he cites reported valuations of ~$100M at seed, ~$500M at Series A, and unconfirmed billion-dollar-plus offers, while noting it is 'probably violating all sorts of terms of service.'
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: A live example of an AI agent monetizing by taking real-world transactional actions (with stored payment credentials), a capability/valuation leap ahead of typical chat-based assistants, but with unresolved ToS/legal risk.
insights.quote: they're probably violating all sorts of terms of service. Um but hey, the thing works.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis reports using an AI agent to auto-edit a YouTube clip into five short vertical clips with captions in about 3 minutes, work he estimates would otherwise cost about $50/hour in freelance video editing and take roughly 3 hours.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete, first-hand productivity multiple (hours to minutes, near-zero marginal cost) for AI agent tooling in media/content operations.
insights.quote: that's a $50 an hour video editor... instead of taking three hours, it took three minutes and was essentially close to free.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts that whichever consumer AI agent product first adds true 'multiplayer mode' -- shared access for team members at comment-only or read-only permission levels, like Google Docs -- will see adoption 'go parabolic.'
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific missing feature (multi-user collaboration) as the likely unlock for mainstream/team adoption of personal AI agents.

insights.claim: The panel recounts that the open-source agent project OpenClaw rose to intense hype and then collapsed in perceived momentum within about one month, after its lead figure was hired into OpenAI; a related project, Moltbook, was reportedly acquired by Meta for roughly $250 million, and the lead figure's own equity was rumored at $200-300M when the company was valued at $300-400M -- implying a possible $1B+ paper value if OpenAI reaches a $2 trillion valuation.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis / Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: Illustrates how quickly open-source AI project momentum can evaporate once a key contributor is acquired by a well-funded lab -- a fragility risk for open ecosystems built around individuals.
insights.quote: I've never seen a project go from everybody embracing it, talking about it to completely toxic and people being like, yeah, you know, I got to go find something else.

insights.claim: Dave McClure cites leaked internal OpenAI commentary from CFO Sarah Friar shifting from 'not ready to IPO' four months ago to targeting an IPO in 2027 or sooner if growth keeps inflecting, tied to weekly active AI-agent user growth that went from about 200K in January to over 1 million a month before this taping, then 5M (May), 6M (July), 10M (later July), 15M (early August), and 20M (late August) -- roughly 4x growth in two months -- alongside a separate claim that OpenAI's revenue growth recently overtook Anthropic's.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Concrete, sourced growth figures showing OpenAI's agent product inflecting sharply, which the company is reportedly using internally to justify accelerating its IPO timeline.
insights.quote: You're talking about 4xing in two months.

insights.claim: Shiel Mohnot's fund led the seed round in Basis, an AI accounting-automation startup he compares to Harvey/Luminance for law, describing it as automating 'the work of a junior accountant'; Kleiner Perkins' Keith Rabois led the Series A and Excel led a recent Series B, with strong usage growth among accounting firms.
insights.speaker: Shiel Mohnot
insights.so_what: AI-for-professional-services (accounting, following law) is being validated by top-tier follow-on investors, suggesting the category is moving from thesis to proof.

insights.claim: Dave McClure highlights MOTU, a Sao Paulo, Brazil-based motorcycle manufacturing and micro-lending company for delivery drivers, as one of his best-performing investments: over $300M in revenue, profitable, and growing 60-70% per year at a reasonable valuation; his firm allocates about 10% of capital to Latin America.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: A reminder that large, profitable, fast-growing non-AI, non-US businesses (emerging-market fintech/lending) remain some of the strongest risk-adjusted returns in venture right now.

insights.claim: Dave McClure also backs EquityBee, a platform offering employee stock-option forward-contract financing that lets departing employees finance and exercise options for liquidity before shares are otherwise available -- a direct bet on the same 'staying private longer' liquidity gap discussed earlier in the show.
insights.speaker: Dave McClure
insights.so_what: Connects a specific portfolio bet to the macro thesis that late-stage illiquidity is a durable, growing market opportunity, not just a talking point.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji's fund wrote a $10M inception check into CuspAI (AI for materials science) at what felt like an aggressive valuation at the time; Kleiner Perkins has since marked it up to $2.6 billion, making it almost a fund returner for his Fund III within about two years.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: A concrete, fast markup example (roughly 2 years to near-fund-returner status) supporting the AI-for-science investment category.

insights.claim: Hussein Kanji says he is most excited not by CuspAI but by a sister investment, Pepone (AI for biology/drug discovery), which has produced a computer-designed drug candidate against prostate cancer now heading into clinical trials, and frames it as the investment most likely to generate outsized fund DPI.
insights.speaker: Hussein Kanji
insights.so_what: A tangible example of AI-designed drug candidates reaching clinical trials, evidence the AI-for-biology thesis is producing real pipeline assets, not just software tools.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis highlights Abacus, an on-prem/sovereign AI company (incubated ~18 months ago) that deploys a single server on-site so regulated industries like banking and healthcare can build private LLMs and agents without sending data to frontier labs, and says it has a waitlist for its product.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: On-prem/sovereign AI for regulated industries is showing real demand (a waitlist), a differentiated angle from consumer/cloud AI plays.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis highlights Micro1, a company he backed at a $10-15M valuation that pivoted from developer-vetting into AI training-data services, hitting $500M in training revenue and a $4 billion valuation this week -- a roughly three-to-four-times fund-returner outcome.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast AI training-data/labeling services have scaled in revenue and valuation, and shows the value of backing a founder willing to pivot business models quickly.
